name: Documents and screens
description: Pictures of paperwork and screens: documents, pages, notes, technical material, app and web screens, capture and wear.

entries.name: receipt
entries.description: Proof that something was already paid for, usually a narrow thermal till slip with a line per item and a total at the bottom. Use [invoice](#invoice) instead when the paper is a request for payment rather than a record of one.

entries.name: contract
entries.description: A binding agreement between parties, laid out in numbered clauses with [signature](#signature) lines at the end. Use it for employment, sale and service agreements alike; a rental one is [lease_agreement](#lease_agreement).

entries.name: form
entries.description: A page built from labelled fields, boxes or ruled lines waiting to be filled in, whether still blank or already completed. Use [application_form](#application_form) or [questionnaire](#questionnaire) when the purpose is clear; otherwise this is the general tag.

entries.name: invoice
entries.description: A demand for payment listing goods or services, amounts, a due date and payment details. Distinguished from [receipt](#receipt), which confirms money already changed hands, and from [quotation](#quotation), which is only an offer.

entries.name: letter
entries.description: Correspondence addressed from one party to another, with a date, a salutation and a sign-off. Covers business post, official notices and private letters. The paper it arrived in is [envelope](#envelope); an internal circular is [memo](#memo).

entries.name: application_form
entries.description: A [form](#form) submitted to ask for something: a job, a visa, a licence, a school place, a bank account. Usually has personal-detail fields at the top and a declaration and [signature](#signature) at the foot.

entries.name: bank_statement
entries.description: A dated list of account transactions with a running or closing balance, issued by a bank or card provider. The giveaway is the transaction [table](#table) with debits and credits; a single charge on its own is an [invoice](#invoice) or [receipt](#receipt).

entries.name: certificate
entries.description: A single decorative sheet attesting to a fact or achievement, typically with a border, a seal and one or two signatures. Diplomas, birth records and awards all sit under it; use the specific tag as well when one fits.

entries.name: envelope
entries.description: The posted wrapper rather than its contents: address block, stamp or franking mark, window, postmark. Use [letter](#letter) for the sheet inside and [shipping_label](#shipping_label) for a parcel's carrier sticker.

entries.name: letterhead
entries.description: The printed identity block at the head of official stationery: sender's name, address and contact line, sometimes repeated as a footer. Tag it when the header itself is the point of the picture, alongside [letter](#letter) or [invoice](#invoice).

entries.name: passport
entries.description: A travel document booklet, most often photographed open at the data page with the photo and machine-readable lines. A stamp or sticker page inside is still this tag unless the entry [permit](#permit) itself is the subject, which is permit.

entries.name: payslip
entries.description: An employer's breakdown of one pay period: gross pay, deductions, tax and net amount. Often photographed for a loan or rental application. Not a [tax_document](#tax_document), which is filed with the authorities rather than issued with wages.

entries.name: report
entries.description: A multi-page written account with headings, findings and often tables or charts: inspection reports, medical write-ups, school reports, annual accounts. Use it when the page is prose and data rather than a fillable [form](#form).

entries.name: tax_document
entries.description: Anything belonging to a tax filing: returns, assessments, withholding statements, notices from the revenue office. Numbered boxes and an official reference are typical. Wage paperwork from the employer is [payslip](#payslip).

entries.name: utility_bill
entries.description: A periodic charge from an electricity, water, gas, phone or internet supplier, often with a consumption [graph](#graph) or meter reading beside the amount due. Use [invoice](#invoice) for ordinary commercial billing and [bank_statement](#bank_statement) for account activity.

entries.name: birth_certificate
entries.description: A civil register extract recording a birth: name, date, place and parents, with a registrar's seal or stamp. Marriage and death extracts from the same registry belong here too; graduation paper is [diploma](#diploma).

entries.name: cheque
entries.description: A written payment order on a bank, with payee, amount in figures and words, date and [signature](#signature), often on patterned security paper. Cancelled and voided ones count too.

entries.name: delivery_note
entries.description: The slip travelling with goods, listing what is in the box without prices, signed off on [receipt](#receipt). Confused with [invoice](#invoice), which carries the money; if it is stuck to the outside of the parcel it is a [shipping_label](#shipping_label).

entries.name: diploma
entries.description: A [certificate](#certificate) of a completed degree, course or qualification, naming the holder, the institution and the date. Often shot framed on a wall. The mark-by-mark record of study is an academic transcript, filed under [report](#report).

entries.name: driver_license
entries.description: A licence to drive, card-sized with a portrait, categories and expiry date, or an older folded paper version. Commonly photographed for rentals and verification.

entries.name: insurance_policy
entries.description: Cover documents naming the insured, the risk, the sum and the exclusions, often with a policy number and a schedule page. A claim [form](#form) is [application_form](#application_form); the renewal demand is [invoice](#invoice).

entries.name: lease_agreement
entries.description: A tenancy or rental [contract](#contract) naming the property, the term and the rent, usually with an inventory or condition schedule attached. A narrower case of contract, worth its own tag because it turns up so often in personal paperwork.

entries.name: ledger
entries.description: Ruled accounting pages of columns and running totals, handwritten in a bound book or printed from an accounts package. A bank's own version of the same idea is [bank_statement](#bank_statement).

entries.name: medical_record
entries.description: Clinical paperwork about a patient: results, discharge letters, vaccination cards, referral notes, imaging reports. Use [prescription](#prescription) for the medicine script and [application_form](#application_form) for an insurance claim.

entries.name: memo
entries.description: A short internal note circulated inside an organisation, headed with to, from, date and subject lines. Shorter and blunter than a [letter](#letter), and unlike [report](#report) it argues nothing at length.

entries.name: official_stamp
entries.description: An inked stamp, embossed seal or wax seal applied to a document to authorise it, often over a [signature](#signature) and in a contrasting colour. Tag it alongside whatever the document is when the mark itself matters.

entries.name: prescription
entries.description: A small printed or handwritten script naming a medicine, dose and prescriber, often on tinted security paper. Test results and clinical notes are [medical_record](#medical_record).

entries.name: purchase_order
entries.description: A buyer's formal order to a supplier, carrying a PO number, line items and agreed prices before anything is delivered or billed. The supplier's answer to it is the [invoice](#invoice); the goods arrive with a [delivery_note](#delivery_note).

entries.name: questionnaire
entries.description: A [form](#form) of questions with tick boxes or rating scales, gathering opinions or facts rather than processing a request. Use [application_form](#application_form) when the paper asks the authority for something instead of asking the reader.

entries.name: quotation
entries.description: A priced offer for work not yet agreed, usually marked valid until a given date. Nothing is owed on it, which is what separates it from [invoice](#invoice), and nothing is ordered, which separates it from [purchase_order](#purchase_order).

entries.name: resume
entries.description: A career summary in dated sections for education and employment, one or two pages, laid out for scanning rather than reading. The [letter](#letter) sent with it is letter; the [form](#form) an employer supplies is [application_form](#application_form).

entries.name: shipping_label
entries.description: A carrier's adhesive label on a parcel: sender and recipient blocks, service class, tracking number and barcode. Tag the paperwork inside the box as [delivery_note](#delivery_note) instead.

entries.name: timesheet
entries.description: A ruled grid of hours worked by day or task, signed off by worker and supervisor. It records the work; [payslip](#payslip) records what was paid for it.

entries.name: warranty
entries.description: A guarantee card or booklet promising repair or replacement for a stated period, usually packed with an appliance and [stamped](#stamped) by the dealer. Keep it apart from [receipt](#receipt), which is only the proof of purchase it references.

entries.name: notarized_document
entries.description: Paperwork carrying a notary's or solicitor's certification: an attestation block, a seal and a register number added to an existing deed, affidavit or copy. Use the underlying tag as well, and [official_stamp](#official_stamp) for the mark alone.

entries.name: badge
entries.description: A worn identity card for a workplace, a conference or a site, showing a name, a role and often a photo, clipped or hung at chest height. The strap it hangs from is [lanyard](#lanyard); a temporary one for a guest is [visitor_pass](#visitor_pass).

entries.name: boarding_pass
entries.description: A pass to board a flight, ferry or sleeper, printed at a desk on flimsy stock with seat, gate and a barcode. A stub for admission or a journey with no seat assigned is [ticket](#ticket); the phone version is [e_ticket](#e_ticket).

entries.name: business_card
entries.description: A pocket-sized card with a name, a role and contact details, usually photographed to keep the details rather than the card. Often shot alone on a desk or fanned in a small stack.

entries.name: driving_licence
entries.description: A licence to drive: card-sized with a portrait, vehicle categories and an expiry date, or an older folded paper sheet. Papers about the vehicle rather than the driver are [vehicle_registration](#vehicle_registration).

entries.name: id_card
entries.description: A card-format identity document carrying a portrait, a name and a number: national ID, works card, resident card. Use the specific tag when the document names itself, such as [driving_licence](#driving_licence) or [student_id](#student_id), and [passport_page](#passport_page) for a booklet.

entries.name: id_photo
entries.description: A passport-style head-and-shoulders portrait on a plain light ground, shot square to the face with a neutral expression, printed as a sheet of four or six. Once it sits inside a document, tag that document instead.

entries.name: passport_page
entries.description: A page of a [passport](#passport) booklet, most often the data page with the portrait and the printed lines at the foot. A page carrying an entry mark is [passport_stamp](#passport_stamp); one carrying a full-page sticker is [visa_page](#visa_page).

entries.name: ticket
entries.description: An admission or travel stub for a cinema, concert, museum, bus or car park, small and often torn or perforated. Rail tickets with a route and a seat are [train_ticket](#train_ticket); a flight document is [boarding_pass](#boarding_pass).

entries.name: baggage_tag
entries.description: The adhesive strip wrapped round a suitcase handle at check-in, with a route, a barcode and a long number, or the stub of it kept by the traveller. Not the owner's own name label tied to the case.

entries.name: e_ticket
entries.description: A [ticket](#ticket) or boarding pass shown on a phone screen or printed from an email, dominated by a barcode or square code and a booking reference. Photographed as a screen or a plain sheet rather than as printed stock.

entries.name: itinerary
entries.description: A printed or emailed plan of a journey listing flights, trains, hotels and times, usually over one or more full pages. It confirms a booking rather than admitting anyone, which is what [boarding_pass](#boarding_pass) does.

entries.name: key_card
entries.description: A blank or lightly printed card that opens a door by magnetic stripe or contactless chip, typically a hotel room key or an office entry card. It carries no portrait, unlike [badge](#badge), and is often shown in its paper sleeve.

entries.name: lanyard
entries.description: The printed neck strap and clip that a [badge](#badge) hangs from, often carrying an event name repeated along its length. Tag it when the strap is legible or is the subject; the card itself is badge.

entries.name: loyalty_card
entries.description: A shop or cafe card that collects points or punched stamps towards a reward, usually with a barcode on the back. Belonging to an organisation rather than a shop scheme is [membership_card](#membership_card).

entries.name: machine_readable_zone
entries.description: The two or three lines of blocky characters and chevrons at the foot of a [passport](#passport) or ID, meant for a scanner. Tag it when those lines are the point of the picture, over [passport_page](#passport_page) or [id_card](#id_card).

entries.name: membership_card
entries.description: A card showing that its holder belongs to a club, union, library or gym, with a member number and often an expiry date. When the card mainly collects points or stamps for purchases, use [loyalty_card](#loyalty_card).

entries.name: parking_permit
entries.description: A card or sticker shown in a windscreen allowing a vehicle to stand in a zone, bay or site, usually dated and numbered. A paid stub from a machine is [ticket](#ticket).

entries.name: passport_stamp
entries.description: An inked border mark in a travel document recording an entry, an exit or a transit, usually dated and often overlapping its neighbours. The whole opened booklet is [passport_page](#passport_page); a pasted authorisation is [visa_page](#visa_page).

entries.name: permit
entries.description: A permission granted by an authority and carried as proof: work permit, building permit, fishing licence, firearms card. Use the narrower tag where one fits, such as [residence_permit](#residence_permit) or [parking_permit](#parking_permit).

entries.name: redacted_id
entries.description: An identity or travel document with numbers, dates or the portrait blacked out, blurred or covered by a finger before sharing. Tag it with whatever the document is, and use it only where the covering is deliberate.

entries.name: residence_permit
entries.description: A card or booklet page allowing a foreign national to live in a country, with a portrait, a status code and a validity period. A sticker permitting entry for a visit is [visa_page](#visa_page).

entries.name: student_id
entries.description: A school or university card with a portrait, an enrolment number and often a term validity sticker. Frequently doubles as a library and canteen card. A card issued by an employer instead is [badge](#badge).

entries.name: train_ticket
entries.description: A rail or coach [ticket](#ticket) showing a route, a date, a class and often a reserved seat, printed on card stock or a long till [receipt](#receipt). A card loaded with fares for repeated journeys is [travel_card](#travel_card).

entries.name: travel_card
entries.description: A reusable card or pass for local transport, loaded with credit or a period of travel and tapped at a gate. Unlike [train_ticket](#train_ticket) it names no single journey, and unlike [ticket](#ticket) it is not surrendered.

entries.name: vaccination_card
entries.description: A small booklet or card recording jabs by date, batch and stamp, often needed for travel or school. Ruled and filled in by hand over years, unlike a printed one-off [certificate](#certificate).

entries.name: vehicle_registration
entries.description: Papers identifying a vehicle rather than its driver: registration [certificate](#certificate), log book, insurance card, roadworthiness sheet, with a plate number and chassis details. The driver's own document is [driving_licence](#driving_licence).

entries.name: visa_page
entries.description: A permission to enter a country, printed as a full-page sticker or foil in a [passport](#passport) with a photo, dates and a machine-readable strip. A card or paper issued separately for a longer stay is [residence_permit](#residence_permit).

entries.name: visitor_pass
entries.description: A temporary pass for a guest at a building or site, often a printed sticker, a dated slip or a plain card marked visitor. Issued for hours or a day, unlike the permanent [badge](#badge) of a member of staff.

entries.name: wristband
entries.description: A paper, fabric or plastic band closed round the wrist to show admission at a festival, a club or a hospital. Photographed on the arm or cut off afterwards. A card worn on the chest instead is [badge](#badge).

entries.name: customs_declaration
entries.description: A short [form](#form) filled in on arrival declaring goods, cash, food or a place of stay, often a coloured card handed out in flight. The permission to enter itself is [visa_page](#visa_page).

entries.name: press_pass
entries.description: Accreditation for a reporter or photographer at an event or venue, with a portrait, an outlet name and dated access markings. Distinguished from an ordinary [badge](#badge) by naming what the holder is allowed to enter.

entries.name: security_hologram
entries.description: The shifting foil patch, laminate or repeated ghost image over an identity document, flaring in the light and often obscuring the print beneath. Tag it alongside the document when catching the effect was the point.

entries.name: social_security_card
entries.description: A plain number card issued by a state for insurance, pensions or tax, carrying a name and a long number and usually no photo. Because it has no portrait it is weak proof of identity by itself.

entries.name: book_page
entries.description: A page from a bound book: body text set in a single measure, with a running head and a folio in the margin. Use it for ordinary interior pages; the opening page naming the work is [title_page](#title_page), and a picture bound in on heavier stock is [illustrated_plate](#illustrated_plate).

entries.name: book_cover
entries.description: The front or back board of a book, carrying the title and author over artwork, cloth or plain board. If the printed paper wrapper is on and is what you can see, tag [dust_jacket](#dust_jacket) instead.

entries.name: comic_page
entries.description: A page divided into panels with gutters between them, speech balloons and caption boxes. Use [manga_page](#manga_page) for the right-to-left [form](#form), [splash_page](#splash_page) for a single full-page panel, [comic_strip](#comic_strip) for a short horizontal run.

entries.name: magazine_page
entries.description: An inside page of a magazine: several columns of body text, a pull quote, pictures bleeding to the trim. The front is [magazine_cover](#magazine_cover); a page torn out and kept loose is [tear_sheet](#tear_sheet).

entries.name: manga_page
entries.description: A page read right to left, with irregular panel shapes, screentone shading and lettering that may run vertically. Use [comic_page](#comic_page) for the left-to-right [form](#form).

entries.name: newspaper_page
entries.description: An inside newspaper page: grey columns of small type, headlines of stepped weights, thin cheap paper. The leading page is [front_page](#front_page) and the columns of tiny set-solid ads are [classified_ads](#classified_ads).

entries.name: poster
entries.description: A large printed sheet made to be hung and read at a distance: big type, one image, broad flat areas of colour. Small handouts are [flyer](#flyer); an advertisement inside a publication is [print_advertisement](#print_advertisement).

entries.name: brochure
entries.description: A folded or stapled sales document of several panels or a few pages, with photographs and short blocks of selling copy. A plain single sheet of information is [leaflet](#leaflet); a cheap event [handout](#handout) is [flyer](#flyer).

entries.name: catalogue_page
entries.description: Goods or works laid out in a grid, each with a picture, a short caption and a number or price. Exhibition and mail-order pages both count; a folded sales sheet with selling copy is [brochure](#brochure).

entries.name: comic_strip
entries.description: A short horizontal run of three or four panels ending on a beat, as printed across a newspaper column or on its own. Panelled storytelling filling a whole page is [comic_page](#comic_page).

entries.name: contents_page
entries.description: A list of chapters, articles or sections against their page numbers, often ruled or dotted across the measure. Found at the front of books and magazines alike; the alphabetical list at the back is [index_page](#index_page).

entries.name: double_page_spread
entries.description: Both open pages shot together, the gutter running down the middle and an image or headline crossing it. Use it when the layout is designed across the two leaves, not for any book that happens to be open.

entries.name: flyer
entries.description: A cheap single-sheet [handout](#handout) for an event or an offer, often one or two colours and heavily typeset. A sheet meant to be pasted up and read at a distance is [poster](#poster).

entries.name: front_page
entries.description: The first page of a newspaper, carrying the masthead, date line, a lead headline and the top stories above and below the fold. Inside pages are [newspaper_page](#newspaper_page); a magazine's front is [magazine_cover](#magazine_cover).

entries.name: leaflet
entries.description: A single sheet, unfolded or folded once, giving information: opening times, instructions, a public notice. Use [flyer](#flyer) when it advertises an event and [brochure](#brochure) when it is thicker and sells something.

entries.name: magazine_cover
entries.description: The front of a magazine, with a masthead across the top, cover lines down the sides and one dominant picture. Distinct from [front_page](#front_page), which leads with headlines and columns of news type.

entries.name: manual_page
entries.description: Instructions in numbered steps with exploded diagrams, part callouts, warning symbols and terse captions. Teaching material with exercises is [textbook_page](#textbook_page); a one-sheet set of instructions is [leaflet](#leaflet).

entries.name: menu
entries.description: A printed list of dishes or drinks with prices, on a card, a folded sheet or a board. Sections and prices set it apart from [catalogue_page](#catalogue_page), which lists goods with pictures.

entries.name: print_advertisement
entries.description: A designed advertisement printed in a publication: one picture, a headline and a logo lockup filling part or all of the page. Use [classified_ads](#classified_ads) for the columned small ads, [poster](#poster) for a sheet made to be hung.

entries.name: programme
entries.description: A booklet or folded sheet for a performance, match or ceremony, listing the running order, cast or teams and carrying advertisements. The sheet that advertised the event beforehand is [flyer](#flyer).

entries.name: textbook_page
entries.description: A teaching page: numbered exercises, labelled diagrams, worked examples and boxed definitions in tinted panels. Continuous prose pages of a book are [book_page](#book_page); step-by-step instructions are [manual_page](#manual_page).

entries.name: title_page
entries.description: The page inside a book giving the full title, author and publisher, set large with generous white space. The dense small-type page of edition and legal detail that usually faces it is [copyright_page](#copyright_page).

entries.name: classified_ads
entries.description: Columns of tiny advertisements set solid and grouped under headings — sales, jobs, notices, personals. Distinct from [print_advertisement](#print_advertisement), which is one designed display ad occupying a block or a whole page.

entries.name: comic_cover
entries.description: The front of a comic issue: a title logo across the top, an issue number and price in a corner, one dramatic scene. Interior panelled pages are [comic_page](#comic_page).

entries.name: copyright_page
entries.description: The small-type page carrying publisher, edition, printing history, cataloguing data and the printing number line. Usually on the back of [title_page](#title_page), and often photographed to record which edition a copy is.

entries.name: dictionary_page
entries.description: Dense reference entries in narrow columns with bold headwords, pronunciations and numbered senses, guide words at the top corners. Use [index_page](#index_page) for a bare list of terms and page numbers.

entries.name: dust_jacket
entries.description: The printed paper wrapper folded around a hardback, with flaps carrying blurb, biography and price. Tag it when the jacket is the thing shown; the board underneath, bare, is [book_cover](#book_cover).

entries.name: illustrated_plate
entries.description: A full-page picture printed apart from the text and bound in, often on heavier or glossier stock with a caption and plate number, sometimes behind tissue. Pictures set into the running text are [book_page](#book_page).

entries.name: index_page
entries.description: Back-matter listing terms alphabetically with page references, set small in two or three narrow columns with indented sub-entries. Distinct from [contents_page](#contents_page), which follows the order of the book and sits at the front.

entries.name: map_sheet
entries.description: A printed [map](#map) with a key, scale bar and grid references, folded flat or bound into an atlas. Use it for the printed sheet only; a mapping application on a display is not this.

entries.name: newsletter
entries.description: A few pages of news for members, staff or subscribers, printed plainly with a nameplate at the top and short dated items below. Denser, larger and daily is [newspaper_page](#newspaper_page).

entries.name: pamphlet
entries.description: A slim stitched or folded booklet arguing a case or explaining a subject, mostly text behind a plain cover. Use [brochure](#brochure) when it sells goods and [leaflet](#leaflet) for a single sheet.

entries.name: puzzle_page
entries.description: A printed grid or set of puzzles — crossword, sudoku, word search — with numbered clues in columns alongside. Partly filled in by hand still counts as this page.

entries.name: recipe_page
entries.description: An ingredient list beside a numbered method, usually with a photograph of the finished dish and a serving count. Equally at home in a cookbook or a magazine, so it stands on its own.

entries.name: sheet_music
entries.description: Printed staves with notes, clefs, dynamics and lyrics set under the melody, bound or loose. Tag the notation itself; the decorated front of a song album is [book_cover](#book_cover).

entries.name: zine
entries.description: A small self-made publication: photocopied, hand-lettered or cut and pasted, stapled through the fold. Distinct from [magazine_page](#magazine_page), which is commercially printed and set on a grid.

entries.name: colophon
entries.description: A short note on how the book was made — typeface, paper, press, print run — set at the very back, sometimes under a printer's device. Not [copyright_page](#copyright_page), which carries the legal and edition detail instead.

entries.name: splash_page
entries.description: A comic page given over to one full-size panel, often the opening scene with the title and credits lettered into the art. An ordinary grid of panels is [comic_page](#comic_page).

entries.name: tear_sheet
entries.description: A single page torn or cut from a publication and kept loose, with ragged edges and the reverse showing through. A page still bound in its magazine is [magazine_page](#magazine_page).

entries.name: handwritten_note
entries.description: Words written by hand on paper, whatever the surface or the purpose. Use it as the general tag whenever somebody's handwriting is the point of the picture, and add the specific one — [diary_page](#diary_page), [shopping_list](#shopping_list), [handwritten_letter](#handwritten_letter) — as well when it fits.

entries.name: doodle
entries.description: Aimless drawing done while thinking — spirals, faces, boxes, cross-hatched patterns — usually in a margin or an empty corner beside real notes. Use [sketched_diagram](#sketched_diagram) when the drawing explains something and [illustrated_note](#illustrated_note) when it is deliberate decoration.

entries.name: notebook_page
entries.description: A page of a bound or spiral notebook, shot open or laid flat. The binding, wire or stitched spine is usually visible. Use [loose_leaf_page](#loose_leaf_page) for a single unbound sheet and [index_card](#index_card) for a small stiff card.

entries.name: signature
entries.description: A name written as a personal mark — on a document, a card, a plaster cast or a signature pad. Looser and faster than the writing around it. Use [book_inscription](#book_inscription) when a message goes with it.

entries.name: sticky_note
entries.description: A small square of adhesive paper carrying a short note, stuck to a page, a screen, a door or a desk. Usually one or two lines. Use [index_card](#index_card) for a stiff card and [planner_page](#planner_page) when the note sits in a dated diary.

entries.name: ballpoint_writing
entries.description: Writing in ballpoint: thin even lines, slightly waxy, with skips and small blobs where the ball reloaded. The everyday default. Use [fountain_pen_writing](#fountain_pen_writing) for wet varied lines and [pencil_writing](#pencil_writing) for grey graphite.

entries.name: diary_page
entries.description: A dated personal entry written by hand, usually running prose rather than a list. A date at the top and first-person text are the giveaways. Use [lecture_notes](#lecture_notes) for study material and [handwritten_letter](#handwritten_letter) for something addressed to someone else.

entries.name: hand_lettering
entries.description: Letters drawn as shapes — outlined, filled, shaded, fitted into a composition — rather than written in one pass. A quote on a chalkboard or a decorated title page is typical. Use [brush_lettering](#brush_lettering) when the strokes swell under a brush.

entries.name: handwritten_letter
entries.description: A [letter](#letter) written out by hand, with a greeting, running text and a sign-off, often on folded stationery. Use [handwritten_note](#handwritten_note) for an unaddressed jotting and [envelope_address](#envelope_address) when the [envelope](#envelope) is what was photographed.

entries.name: lecture_notes
entries.description: Notes taken while listening — dense, abbreviated, headed by a date or a topic, full of arrows and underlinings. Use [meeting_notes](#meeting_notes) when the subject is a discussion between people and [diary_page](#diary_page) for personal entries.

entries.name: pencil_writing
entries.description: Grey graphite writing, often smudged or half erased with the ghost of the old words still showing. Use [ballpoint_writing](#ballpoint_writing) or [fountain_pen_writing](#fountain_pen_writing) when the marks are ink.

entries.name: ruled_paper
entries.description: Paper printed with horizontal writing lines, sometimes with a red margin rule down the left. Describes the sheet rather than what is on it, so pair it with [handwritten_note](#handwritten_note). Use [graph_paper](#graph_paper) for a full grid.

entries.name: shopping_list
entries.description: A short list of things to buy — nouns and quantities on a scrap of paper, an [envelope](#envelope) back or a phone screen. Distinguished from [to-do_list](#to-do_list) by the entries being goods rather than tasks.

entries.name: sketched_diagram
entries.description: A drawing made to explain something — boxes and arrows, a floor plan, a circuit, a sequence of steps — drawn freehand rather than plotted. Use [doodle](#doodle) for aimless drawing and [mind_map](#mind_map) when everything radiates from one central idea.

entries.name: to-do_list
entries.description: Tasks written out one per line, often behind dashes or empty boxes, some of them ticked off. Use [shopping_list](#shopping_list) when the entries are goods to buy, and [planner_page](#planner_page) when the tasks are hung on dated days.

entries.name: book_inscription
entries.description: A dedication written by hand on the flyleaf or title page of a book — a name, a date, a line of greeting. Use [signature](#signature) when only a name was left and [handwritten_note](#handwritten_note) for a reader's own jottings elsewhere in the book.

entries.name: brush_lettering
entries.description: Lettering made with a brush or brush pen, so stroke width swells and tapers with pressure and edges go dry at the ends. Use [marker_writing](#marker_writing) for flat felt-tip strokes.

entries.name: child's_handwriting
entries.description: Large, wobbling letters of uneven size and spacing, sometimes with reversed letters or a drawing worked in. Use [penmanship_practice](#penmanship_practice) when the page is rows of repeated letters for training.

entries.name: dot_grid_paper
entries.description: Paper marked with a faint grid of dots instead of lines, common in modern notebooks because the dots vanish in a photograph of the writing. Use [graph_paper](#graph_paper) when the grid is drawn as full lines.

entries.name: envelope_address
entries.description: An address written by hand across an [envelope](#envelope) or parcel, often beside stamps and a postmark. Tag it for the writing on the wrapper; the [letter](#letter) inside is [handwritten_letter](#handwritten_letter).

entries.name: flashcard
entries.description: A card made for memorising: a word, phrase or question on one side and its answer on the other. Usually shown as a pair or a deck. Use [index_card](#index_card) for a card holding ordinary notes.

entries.name: fountain_pen_writing
entries.description: Nib writing with wet lines of varying weight, ink pooled at the ends of strokes and sometimes feathering into the paper. Use [ballpoint_writing](#ballpoint_writing) for flat even lines.

entries.name: graded_schoolwork
entries.description: A pupil's page worked over by a teacher: ticks, red corrections, a mark or grade circled at the top. The two different hands on one page are the giveaway. Use [handwritten_equations](#handwritten_equations) for untouched working alone.

entries.name: graph_paper
entries.description: Paper printed with a square grid, used for plots, diagrams and neat working. Use [ruled_paper](#ruled_paper) for plain horizontal lines and [dot_grid_paper](#dot_grid_paper) when only the intersections are marked.

entries.name: handwritten_equations
entries.description: Mathematics or chemistry worked out by hand: fractions, integrals, formulas, a page of algebra with crossings-out. Often on [graph_paper](#graph_paper). Use [lecture_notes](#lecture_notes) when prose and headings dominate the page instead.

entries.name: handwritten_recipe
entries.description: Cooking instructions copied out by hand, ingredients listed above a method, often on a card and often stained. A recipe set in print in a book or magazine is not this tag.

entries.name: illustrated_note
entries.description: Notes deliberately combined with small drawings, banners and decorated headings, neat and meant to be looked at. Unlike a [doodle](#doodle) it is planned; unlike [hand_lettering](#hand_lettering) the words still carry information.

entries.name: index_card
entries.description: A small stiff card, blank or ruled, carrying one note, one recipe or one address, often shot in a stack or pinned up. Use [flashcard](#flashcard) when it is a question-and-answer pair for learning.

entries.name: loose_leaf_page
entries.description: A single unbound sheet of writing paper, often punched for a ring binder or ragged where it was torn out. Choose [notebook_page](#notebook_page) when the binding is still attached and visible.

entries.name: marker_writing
entries.description: Thick felt-tip or permanent-marker strokes, opaque and flat-edged, the way a box, a label or a hand-made sign gets written. Use [brush_lettering](#brush_lettering) when the stroke tapers with pressure.

entries.name: meeting_notes
entries.description: Jottings made during a discussion: names, decisions, actions, arrows joining them. Shorter and messier than [lecture_notes](#lecture_notes). A typed formal record of proceedings is office paperwork rather than this.

entries.name: mind_map
entries.description: Ideas written in bubbles or on branches radiating out from one word in the middle. Drawn on paper or in software. Use [sketched_diagram](#sketched_diagram) for a technical drawing and [outline](#outline) for notes stepped down the page.

entries.name: outline
entries.description: Notes built as indented levels, headings with sub-points stepped in beneath them. The staircase of indents is the giveaway. Use [mind_map](#mind_map) for a radiating arrangement and [lecture_notes](#lecture_notes) for a straight run of jottings.

entries.name: planner_page
entries.description: A dated diary or planner spread — days ruled into columns or boxes with appointments written in, sometimes colour-coded. Use [diary_page](#diary_page) for written personal entries and [to-do_list](#to-do_list) for a bare list of tasks.

entries.name: postcard_message
entries.description: The written side of a postcard: a few cramped lines on the left, an address on the right, usually a stamp in the corner. Use [handwritten_letter](#handwritten_letter) for a full [letter](#letter) on stationery.

entries.name: scrapbook_page
entries.description: A page with photographs, tickets or cuttings pasted down and captions written around them by hand. Use [illustrated_note](#illustrated_note) when the drawing is on the page rather than stuck to it.

entries.name: address_book_page
entries.description: A page of names with addresses and numbers written beside them, often thumb-indexed by [letter](#letter) and amended over years in different pens. Use [planner_page](#planner_page) for a dated diary spread.

entries.name: handwritten_sheet_music
entries.description: Staves and notes drawn by hand — a manuscript or a sketch of a tune, usually with corrections. Engraved or printed music is not this tag.

entries.name: napkin_sketch
entries.description: An idea drawn or written on whatever was to hand — a napkin, a coaster, a [receipt](#receipt) back, an [envelope](#envelope). The improvised surface is the point. Use [notebook_page](#notebook_page) or [loose_leaf_page](#loose_leaf_page) for proper writing paper.

entries.name: penmanship_practice
entries.description: Letters or words repeated in rows to train the hand, usually between guide lines on a copybook sheet. The repetition is the giveaway. Use [child's_handwriting](#child's_handwriting) for ordinary writing by a beginner.

entries.name: map
entries.description: A drawn representation of ground seen from above, at any scale, with place names, borders or routes. Use the narrower [topographic_map](#topographic_map), [street_map](#street_map) or [transit_map](#transit_map) where one fits, and [site_plan](#site_plan) for a single property.

entries.name: blueprint
entries.description: A technical drawing reproduced as white lines on a deep blue ground, or any drawing imitating that look. The word is often used loosely for any plan; keep this tag for the blue-and-white appearance and use [technical_drawing](#technical_drawing) otherwise.

entries.name: floor_plan
entries.description: A building drawn from directly above with the walls cut through, showing rooms, doors and fixtures. Room dimensions and furniture symbols are typical. For the outside face of a building drawn flat, use [elevation_drawing](#elevation_drawing).

entries.name: flowchart
entries.description: A procedure drawn as boxes and arrows, with diamonds for yes/no decisions and branches rejoining downstream. Reads as a sequence in time. A [block_diagram](#block_diagram) shows structure instead, and an [org_chart](#org_chart) shows reporting lines.

entries.name: graph
entries.description: Numbers plotted against axes so a shape can be read off them, with tick marks, labels and often a legend. Use [bar_chart](#bar_chart), [line_graph](#line_graph), [pie_chart](#pie_chart) or [scatter_plot](#scatter_plot) when the plot is clearly one of those.

entries.name: labelled_diagram
entries.description: Any illustration whose parts are named by callout lines, leader arrows or letters keyed to a list. The labelling is the point. Combine with [anatomical_diagram](#anatomical_diagram), [exploded_view](#exploded_view) or [map](#map) where one of those also applies.

entries.name: schematic
entries.description: A diagram using standard symbols for components and lines for connections, showing how something works rather than how it is laid out physically. Most often electronic. Use [wiring_diagram](#wiring_diagram) when the drawing tracks actual cables and terminals.

entries.name: spreadsheet
entries.description: A working grid of cells with lettered columns, numbered rows and formulas or totals, whether printed out or ruled by hand in a [ledger](#ledger) book. Use [table](#table) for a plain typeset table with no cell grid.

entries.name: table
entries.description: Information laid out in ruled rows and columns with a header row, printed or drawn. Reference tables, results, price lists. Use [spreadsheet](#spreadsheet) when cell grid lines, row numbers and column letters make it a working sheet.

entries.name: technical_drawing
entries.description: A precise line drawing of an object or structure, drawn to scale with clean linework and no shading. Use it for the general case; reach for [floor_plan](#floor_plan), [schematic](#schematic) or [exploded_view](#exploded_view) when the drawing is one of those specific kinds.

entries.name: bar_chart
entries.description: Values drawn as rectangles from a baseline, upright or on their side, one per category. Includes stacked and grouped bars. Use histogram wording only loosely; for continuous ranges of a single variable, a histogram is the better description.

entries.name: block_diagram
entries.description: Labelled boxes joined by arrows, each box a subsystem rather than a component. Shows how signal or data moves at a coarse level. Use [flowchart](#flowchart) when the boxes are steps in a procedure and decisions branch.

entries.name: checklist
entries.description: A list of items with boxes, ticks or crossings-out beside them, printed or handwritten. Inspection sheets, packing lists, to-do slips. Use [table](#table) when the rows carry data rather than things to be completed.

entries.name: cross_section
entries.description: An object or structure shown as if sliced through, with the cut surfaces usually hatched. Reveals internal layers or construction. Use [cutaway_view](#cutaway_view) instead when only part of the outer shell is peeled away.

entries.name: exploded_view
entries.description: Parts of an assembly drawn pulled apart along their axes of fit, often with thin lines showing where each piece goes. Standard in repair and assembly documents. Pair with [instruction_sheet](#instruction_sheet) when numbered steps accompany it.

entries.name: infographic
entries.description: A designed panel combining figures, small charts, icons and short text into one explanatory picture. The styling and layout carry as much meaning as the numbers. Use [graph](#graph) for a plain plot with axes and nothing else.

entries.name: instruction_sheet
entries.description: A [leaflet](#leaflet) or sheet of numbered steps for assembling, fitting or operating something, usually wordless drawings or terse captions. Often carries an [exploded_view](#exploded_view). Use [checklist](#checklist) when the point is ticking items off.

entries.name: line_graph
entries.description: Points joined into a continuous line across the axes, usually to show change over time. Several series may share the plot. Use [scatter_plot](#scatter_plot) when the points are left unconnected.

entries.name: musical_notation
entries.description: Music written on five-line staves with clefs, note heads and bar lines, printed or handwritten. Covers scores, parts and manuscript paper. Use [tablature](#tablature) for the string-and-fret grids guitarists read.

entries.name: pie_chart
entries.description: A circle cut into wedges by share of a total, usually with percentages or a colour key. Includes ring and doughnut variants. Use [bar_chart](#bar_chart) for comparisons that are not parts of one whole.

entries.name: recipe_card
entries.description: A single card or slip holding one recipe, ingredients above and method below, often handwritten and kitchen-stained. The card format is the distinction; a recipe printed within a book or magazine belongs elsewhere.

entries.name: street_map
entries.description: A [map](#map) of a town or district drawn around its roads, blocks and named landmarks. Includes printed city plans and drawn navigation maps. Use [transit_map](#transit_map) for the simplified line diagrams of a rail or bus network.

entries.name: timetable
entries.description: Times arranged in a grid against services, rooms or days: departures, lesson periods, shift rotas. Use [table](#table) for tabular data that is not scheduled by time, and [gantt_chart](#gantt_chart) for durations drawn as bars.

entries.name: topographic_map
entries.description: A [map](#map) showing relief with contour lines, spot heights and shaded slopes, usually with a grid overlay. Made for walking and survey work. Use [street_map](#street_map) when roads and addresses are the point and terrain is absent.

entries.name: wiring_diagram
entries.description: A drawing of real cabling: wire colours, connector pins and terminal positions as they are physically installed. Used for fitting and fault-finding. A [schematic](#schematic) shows the same circuit logically, without caring where the wires run.

entries.name: anatomical_diagram
entries.description: A body, organ or organism drawn for study, with structures named and often colour-coded by system. Includes plant and animal anatomy. Use [scientific_illustration](#scientific_illustration) for specimen drawings made to record appearance rather than to teach parts.

entries.name: cutaway_view
entries.description: A drawing with part of the outer casing removed so the workings inside are visible, the rest of the object left whole. Common in machinery and vehicle illustration. Differs from [cross_section](#cross_section), which cuts cleanly through the entire object.

entries.name: datasheet
entries.description: A specification document listing a part's ratings, dimensions and pin functions in dense tables, usually with a small [outline](#outline) drawing. Written for selection and fitting, not for operating. Use [instruction_sheet](#instruction_sheet) for step-by-step guidance.

entries.name: elevation_drawing
entries.description: A building or object drawn flat from one side, with no perspective, showing the face as it would measure. Often labelled north, south, front or rear. Distinct from [floor_plan](#floor_plan), which looks straight down.

entries.name: family_tree
entries.description: Generations of a family drawn as connected names, with marriage bars and descent lines, sometimes with dates. Includes hand-drawn genealogies. Use [org_chart](#org_chart) for a workplace hierarchy.

entries.name: isometric_drawing
entries.description: A three-dimensional view drawn on fixed angled axes with no perspective convergence, so parallel edges stay parallel and lengths stay measurable. Recognisable by the even 30-degree slant. Use [technical_drawing](#technical_drawing) for flat single-face views.

entries.name: map_legend
entries.description: The key panel explaining what a document's symbols, colours and line styles mean, often beside a scale bar and north arrow. Tag it when the key is readable or is what the picture is of, not merely a corner of a wider sheet.

entries.name: network_diagram
entries.description: Machines, routers and links drawn as icons joined by lines, often with addresses or zone boundaries. Covers both drawn network maps and topology sketches. Use [block_diagram](#block_diagram) for non-network systems.

entries.name: org_chart
entries.description: Named boxes connected downward to show who reports to whom in an organisation. Use [family_tree](#family_tree) for descent and marriage, and [flowchart](#flowchart) when the connections are steps rather than people.

entries.name: patent_drawing
entries.description: A black-and-white line illustration in the style filings require: hatched shading, numbered reference marks and figure captions, no colour or photography. Recognisable even without the surrounding text. Use [technical_drawing](#technical_drawing) for ordinary engineering sheets.

entries.name: scatter_plot
entries.description: Individual points placed by two measured values, sometimes with a fitted trend line through the cloud. The spread is the message. Use [line_graph](#line_graph) when the points are joined into a path.

entries.name: scientific_illustration
entries.description: A careful drawing or painting of a specimen or phenomenon made as a record: botanical plates, insect studies, geological sections. Accuracy outranks style. Use [anatomical_diagram](#anatomical_diagram) when internal structure is the subject and parts are named.

entries.name: site_plan
entries.description: A plot of land seen from above with the building footprint, boundaries, access roads and landscaping marked. Wider in scope than [floor_plan](#floor_plan) and usually carrying a north arrow. Use [map](#map) for anything covering a whole district or larger.

entries.name: star_chart
entries.description: The night sky drawn as a [map](#map), with stars as graded dots, constellation lines and coordinate grids. Includes planispheres and printed sky atlases. Not a photograph of the sky, which belongs with astrophotography.

entries.name: timeline_diagram
entries.description: Events placed along a dated line or band, in order, with labels above or below. Historical, project or biographical. Use [gantt_chart](#gantt_chart) when tasks have bars with start and end dates.

entries.name: title_block
entries.description: The ruled box in the corner of a drawing sheet holding the project name, scale, drawing number, date and revisions. Tag it when that panel is legible or is the subject of the picture, not merely present.

entries.name: transit_map
entries.description: A network of routes drawn as coloured lines with station ticks, angles snapped to 45 or 90 degrees and geography deliberately distorted. Legibility beats accuracy. A [street_map](#street_map) keeps true distances and shapes.

entries.name: venn_diagram
entries.description: Overlapping circles with labels in the shared and unshared regions, showing what two or three sets have in common. Small and instantly recognisable. Use [block_diagram](#block_diagram) for boxes-and-arrows relationships instead.

entries.name: weather_map
entries.description: A region overlaid with meteorological data: isobars, fronts, temperature bands, rain radar or cloud cover. Includes broadcast graphics and printed synoptic charts. Use [map](#map) alone when the overlay is not weather.

entries.name: gantt_chart
entries.description: A schedule drawn as horizontal bars along a date axis, one row per task, with dependencies and milestones marked. Use [timeline_diagram](#timeline_diagram) for a plain sequence of events with no task rows or durations.

entries.name: nautical_chart
entries.description: A [map](#map) of water for navigation: depth soundings, seabed notes, buoys, lights and compass roses, with the land left mostly blank. Use [star_chart](#star_chart) for the sky and [topographic_map](#topographic_map) for land relief.

entries.name: pcb_layout
entries.description: The artwork of a printed circuit board: copper tracks, pads, silkscreen outlines and board edge, usually in flat colours per layer. Tag the drawing, not a photograph of a finished board. The circuit's logic belongs on [schematic](#schematic).

entries.name: periodic_table
entries.description: The elements laid out in their familiar stepped grid, cells coloured by group and carrying symbol, number and mass. Instantly recognisable by shape alone. Use [table](#table) for any other reference grid.

entries.name: sewing_pattern
entries.description: Full-size garment pieces printed on thin paper with cutting lines, notches, darts and grain arrows, often overlapping in several sizes. Use [technical_drawing](#technical_drawing) for a scaled construction sketch rather than a cuttable sheet.

entries.name: tablature
entries.description: Music written as fret or hole numbers on lines standing for strings, telling the player where to put fingers rather than which pitch to sound. Use [musical_notation](#musical_notation) for ordinary staves and note heads.

entries.name: screenshot
entries.description: A picture captured by the machine itself rather than by a camera: pixel-exact, no lens blur, no page edges. Use it for any captured screen. If the screen was photographed instead, use [photo_of_a_screen](#photo_of_a_screen).

entries.name: browser_window
entries.description: The browser's own frame is visible: tab strip, address bar, back and forward controls. Use it whenever that chrome is in the picture, including in a rendered mockup; for the page content alone use [web_page_screenshot](#web_page_screenshot).

entries.name: code_editor
entries.description: Source code open for editing, with line numbers, a file tree or tab bar and usually [syntax_highlighting](#syntax_highlighting). Use [terminal_window](#terminal_window) for a shell prompt and [diff_view](#diff_view) when two versions are shown side by side.

entries.name: dark_mode_ui
entries.description: An interface drawn light-on-dark: dark window backgrounds, pale text, muted accents. Worth tagging when the theme carries the look of the capture; a [terminal_window](#terminal_window) is dark by default and rarely needs it.

entries.name: desktop_screenshot
entries.description: A capture of a whole computer desktop, usually showing wallpaper, icons and a [taskbar](#taskbar) or dock behind any open windows. Use it for the full screen; a single window on a plain background is better described by the window's own tag.

entries.name: terminal_window
entries.description: A monospaced console: a prompt, typed commands and their output, usually light text on a dark ground. Use [code_editor](#code_editor) for a file being written with a gutter and tabs, even when it also shows monospaced text.

entries.name: web_page_screenshot
entries.description: A capture of a page rendered in a browser, whether or not the browser chrome is included. Add [browser_window](#browser_window) when the address bar and tabs are visible; use [landing_page](#landing_page) or [search_results_page](#search_results_page) for what kind of page it is.

entries.name: chat_window
entries.description: A conversation as stacked message bubbles or lines with a compose box at the bottom, sometimes a channel list beside it. Use [email_client](#email_client) for threaded mail with subjects and an inbox list.

entries.name: context_menu
entries.description: A small list of commands opened at the pointer, typically by a right-click, floating over the interface underneath. Use [modal_dialog](#modal_dialog) for a centred box that blocks the window, and [command_palette](#command_palette) for a searchable command list.

entries.name: dashboard_ui
entries.description: A signed-in overview screen: tiles of numbers, small charts and status cards laid out in a grid. Use [data_table](#data_table) when the screen is one long [table](#table) of rows, and [landing_page](#landing_page) for a public marketing page.

entries.name: data_table
entries.description: Rows and columns with headers, sorting arrows and often pagination underneath, inside an application or page. Use [spreadsheet_view](#spreadsheet_view) for a cell grid with lettered columns and a formula bar.

entries.name: desktop_wallpaper
entries.description: The background image behind the icons and windows is a visible part of the picture. Use it when the wallpaper is what the capture is about or is largely uncovered; a screen filled with windows does not need it.

entries.name: email_client
entries.description: A mail program or webmail screen: folder list, message list with senders and subjects, and a reading pane or compose window. Use [chat_window](#chat_window) for short back-and-forth messages without subjects.

entries.name: error_dialog
entries.description: A dialog reporting that something failed, usually with a warning icon and a code or message. Use [crash_screen](#crash_screen) when the whole system has stopped, and [error_message](#error_message) for error text shown inline rather than in a box.

entries.name: error_message
entries.description: Failure text shown in place: a red line under a [form](#form) field, a stack trace in a [terminal_window](#terminal_window), a red banner across a page. Distinct from [error_dialog](#error_dialog), which is a separate box the user must dismiss.

entries.name: file_manager
entries.description: A window listing files and folders, as icons or as a detail list with size and date columns, with a path or sidebar of locations. Use [spreadsheet_view](#spreadsheet_view) for a grid of cells, not for this kind of file listing.

entries.name: landing_page
entries.description: A marketing page built to be arrived at: a large headline, a hero image, a call-to-action button and sections down the page. Use [dashboard_ui](#dashboard_ui) for a signed-in working screen rather than a page selling something.

entries.name: login_screen
entries.description: A sign-in prompt with username and password fields, or a full-screen lock screen with a clock and user picture. Use [web_form](#web_form) for a longer page of fields, and [paywall](#paywall) for a block asking for payment rather than credentials.

entries.name: modal_dialog
entries.description: A box in front of a dimmed or inert window asking for a choice, with buttons such as OK and Cancel. Use [error_dialog](#error_dialog) when it reports a failure, and [context_menu](#context_menu) for a [menu](#menu) opened at the pointer instead.

entries.name: navigation_bar
entries.description: The horizontal bar of links across the top of a site, with a logo at one end and often a search field or account button. Use [sidebar_navigation](#sidebar_navigation) for a vertical list down the side.

entries.name: photo_of_a_screen
entries.description: A monitor, laptop or television photographed with a camera, so the picture carries moire, reflections, a slight keystone and visible bezel. Distinct from [screenshot](#screenshot), which is captured by the machine and has none of those.

entries.name: progress_bar
entries.description: A filling bar, percentage or spinner showing that work is under way — a copy, a download, an install. Tag it when the waiting state is what the picture shows, not merely because a thin bar sits somewhere on screen.

entries.name: search_results_page
entries.description: A query in a search box above a list of results — links, snippets, thumbnails or product cards with filters down one side. Use [data_table](#data_table) for a plain tabular listing with column headers.

entries.name: settings_panel
entries.description: A preferences screen: rows of toggles, checkboxes, dropdowns and text fields, often with a category list down one side. Use it for any options page, desktop or web; a page collecting data to submit is a [web_form](#web_form).

entries.name: sidebar_navigation
entries.description: A vertical column of sections or folders down one edge of an application or site, the working area beside it. Use [navigation_bar](#navigation_bar) for a horizontal strip and [file_manager](#file_manager) when the sidebar lists disks and folders.

entries.name: spreadsheet_view
entries.description: A grid of cells with lettered columns, numbered rows, a formula bar and sheet tabs along the bottom. Distinct from [data_table](#data_table), which is an application's own list of records with no cell references.

entries.name: syntax_highlighting
entries.description: Code coloured by token — keywords, strings and comments in different hues. Worth tagging when the colouring is the visual character of the picture; it appears in a [code_editor](#code_editor), a [terminal_window](#terminal_window) or a page of documentation alike.

entries.name: taskbar
entries.description: The persistent strip of running applications, launchers, clock and status icons along an edge of the desktop. Covers a bottom taskbar, a side panel and a macOS-style dock alike; it usually appears inside a [desktop_screenshot](#desktop_screenshot).

entries.name: video_call_grid
entries.description: A conferencing screen showing participants as tiles or one speaker with a filmstrip, plus mute and leave controls. Tag the interface, not the people; a plain recorded video with no controls does not belong here.

entries.name: web_form
entries.description: A page of fields to fill in and submit: labelled text boxes, dropdowns, checkboxes and a submit button. Use [login_screen](#login_screen) for a bare sign-in prompt and [settings_panel](#settings_panel) for options that save as you change them.

entries.name: window_title_bar
entries.description: The strip at the top of an application window carrying its name and the close, minimise and zoom controls. Tag it when the window frame itself is the point; for the panel inside, use the tag for that panel.

entries.name: 404_page
entries.description: A page saying the address does not exist, usually a big number, a short apology and a link home. Use it for other server error pages too; a browser's own no-connection screen counts as well.

entries.name: browser_devtools
entries.description: The developer panel docked inside a browser: element tree, styles, network list or console, with the page squeezed beside it. Tag both this and the page tags when the rendered page is also visible.

entries.name: command_palette
entries.description: A search field opened over the interface listing commands or files as you type, common in editors and web apps. Distinct from [context_menu](#context_menu), which is a fixed list at the pointer with nothing to type into.

entries.name: cookie_banner
entries.description: A consent strip or box over a page offering to accept or manage tracking, usually along the bottom or as a centred overlay. Use [paywall](#paywall) for a block demanding payment and [modal_dialog](#modal_dialog) for an ordinary application dialog.

entries.name: crash_screen
entries.description: The whole machine has stopped and says so: a full-screen stop message, a kernel panic, a frozen or corrupted display. Use [error_dialog](#error_dialog) for a failure the running system reports in an ordinary box.

entries.name: diff_view
entries.description: Two versions of a text shown against each other, with added lines in green and removed lines in red, side by side or interleaved. Distinct from a plain [code_editor](#code_editor), which shows one version with no change marks.

entries.name: installer_window
entries.description: A step-by-step setup wizard: licence text, install location, Next and Back buttons, often a [progress_bar](#progress_bar) at the end. Use it also for drag-to-install disk image windows and package manager screens.

entries.name: notification_toast
entries.description: A small message card that slides in at a screen corner and disappears on its own, carrying an app icon and a line of text. Unlike [modal_dialog](#modal_dialog) it blocks nothing and often needs no answer.

entries.name: paywall
entries.description: Content cut off behind a subscribe or pay prompt, often with the article fading out under the box. Distinct from [login_screen](#login_screen), which asks who you are rather than for money.

entries.name: wireframe_mockup
entries.description: A grey-box design of a screen: placeholder blocks, crossed rectangles for images and lorem text, no real content or colour. Distinct from a [screenshot](#screenshot) of a working interface, however plain that interface is.

entries.name: boot_screen
entries.description: What a machine shows before its desktop arrives: a firmware or BIOS [menu](#menu), a boot loader list, scrolling start-up text, a logo with a spinner. Usually plain text on black, with no window frame anywhere.

entries.name: device_mockup
entries.description: A screen placed inside a drawn or photographed laptop, monitor or tablet, often angled with a soft shadow on a plain ground. The screen content is composited in, which separates it from [photo_of_a_screen](#photo_of_a_screen).

entries.name: chat_log
entries.description: A conversation thread on a phone: alternating messages up the screen with a compose field at the bottom. Covers texts and messenger apps alike; use [comment_thread](#comment_thread) for replies hanging under a public post.

entries.name: mobile_screenshot
entries.description: A capture taken on a phone, tall and narrow with a status bar across the top. Use this for anything shot on a handset; use [tablet_screenshot](#tablet_screenshot) for the wider slate proportions and [photo_of_a_screen](#photo_of_a_screen) when a camera photographed the display instead.

entries.name: app_interface
entries.description: A screen from inside a touch app: a header, scrolling content, and controls sized for a thumb. Use it when nothing more specific fits; prefer [chat_log](#chat_log), [map_screen](#map_screen), [camera_viewfinder](#camera_viewfinder) and the like when the app's purpose is obvious.

entries.name: camera_roll
entries.description: The photo library as a grid of thumbnails, often with date headings and a select button. Tag a single picture opened full screen with its share and delete bar the same way; [camera_viewfinder](#camera_viewfinder) is the live camera instead.

entries.name: lock_screen
entries.description: The screen shown before unlocking: a large clock and date over the wallpaper, often with notification cards stacked below. If the phone is asking for a passcode or fingerprint the same tag applies; use [login_screen](#login_screen) for account sign-in inside an app.

entries.name: map_screen
entries.description: A [map](#map) app in use: streets or terrain under pins, a search field and a blue dot for the viewer. Use [map_sheet](#map_sheet) for a printed or scanned map, and [turn_by_turn_navigation](#turn_by_turn_navigation) when a route is being followed.

entries.name: message_bubbles
entries.description: The rounded speech bubbles themselves, one colour for the sender and another for the recipient, with timestamps between runs. Tag it when the bubbles are the subject — a crop of two or three messages rather than a whole [chat_log](#chat_log).

entries.name: phone_home_screen
entries.description: The launcher: wallpaper behind rows of app icons, usually with a dock along the bottom. Use [app_icon_grid](#app_icon_grid) for a dense full-page grid with no wallpaper showing, and [lock_screen](#lock_screen) for the screen before unlocking.

entries.name: push_notification
entries.description: A single notification card: app icon, title, a line or two of text, arriving as a banner at the top or resting on the lock screen. Use [notification_shade](#notification_shade) when the whole pulled-down list is shown.

entries.name: social_media_post
entries.description: A single post as it appears in an app: avatar and handle at the top, body or picture below, like and reply counts underneath. Use [social_feed](#social_feed) when several posts scroll together and [comment_thread](#comment_thread) when the replies dominate.

entries.name: status_bar
entries.description: The thin strip at the top of a phone screen carrying the clock, signal bars, wifi and battery. Tag it when that strip is legible and matters — it dates a shot and proves the capture came off a device rather than a mockup.

entries.name: app_icon_grid
entries.description: A page of nothing but app icons with their labels, filling the screen edge to edge. This is the app drawer or a folder opened out, as opposed to [phone_home_screen](#phone_home_screen) where wallpaper and widgets share the space.

entries.name: bottom_tab_bar
entries.description: The row of three to five icons pinned along the bottom of an app for switching sections, one of them highlighted. Tag the bar itself; [sidebar_navigation](#sidebar_navigation) covers the vertical equivalent on wider screens.

entries.name: camera_viewfinder
entries.description: The camera app live: the scene fills the frame with a shutter button, mode strip and flash toggle drawn over it. The picture underneath is a preview, not a taken photograph — a saved shot belongs in [camera_roll](#camera_roll).

entries.name: comment_thread
entries.description: Replies stacked under a post, indented into branches with vote or like counts. Public and one-to-many, unlike [chat_log](#chat_log), which is a private back-and-forth with a compose field at the bottom.

entries.name: group_chat
entries.description: A thread with three or more participants: names or avatars above each incoming message and a group title in the header. Use [chat_log](#chat_log) for a one-to-one conversation.

entries.name: music_player_screen
entries.description: The now-playing view: cover art, track and artist, a scrub bar and transport buttons. Use it for podcast players too; a list of tracks without the large artwork is better tagged [app_interface](#app_interface).

entries.name: notification_shade
entries.description: The tray pulled down from the top edge, a stack of notification cards often over quick toggles for wifi and brightness. Tag a single card on its own as [push_notification](#push_notification) instead.

entries.name: on_screen_keyboard
entries.description: The software keyboard occupying the lower half of the screen, often with a suggestion strip above it. Its presence usually means a field is being typed into; use emoji_picker only when the emoji panel has replaced the letters.

entries.name: onboarding_screen
entries.description: One card of a first-run walkthrough: an illustration, a short line of copy, page dots and a Next or Skip button. Use [permission_prompt](#permission_prompt) for the system dialog asking for access, which often follows straight after.

entries.name: permission_prompt
entries.description: The system alert asking to allow camera, location, microphone or notifications, with Allow and Don't Allow beneath. It is the operating system speaking over the app, unlike [modal_dialog](#modal_dialog) which belongs to the app itself.

entries.name: social_feed
entries.description: A scrolling column of posts from different accounts, cut off at top and bottom. The plural of [social_media_post](#social_media_post); if one post fills the screen with its replies, tag [comment_thread](#comment_thread) instead.

entries.name: social_media_profile
entries.description: An account page: banner, avatar, display name and bio over follower counts and a grid or list of that person's posts. Distinct from [social_media_post](#social_media_post), which is one item out of the feed.

entries.name: tablet_screenshot
entries.description: A capture from a tablet: touch interface like a phone's, but wide enough for two panes or a sidebar. Distinguish from [mobile_screenshot](#mobile_screenshot) by proportion and layout, and from [desktop_screenshot](#desktop_screenshot) by the absence of window chrome.

entries.name: turn_by_turn_navigation
entries.description: Navigation running: a tilted road view with the next manoeuvre arrow at the top and arrival time along the bottom. Use [map_screen](#map_screen) for browsing a [map](#map) with no active route.

entries.name: video_call_screen
entries.description: A video call on a handset: the other person filling the frame with the viewer's own camera in a small inset corner. Use [video_call_grid](#video_call_grid) for the many-tile desktop layout and [call_screen](#call_screen) for audio only.

entries.name: app_store_page
entries.description: An app's listing: icon, name, install button, rating and a row of swipeable preview shots. Note that the previews inside it are themselves screenshots — tag what the page is, not what it depicts.

entries.name: app_switcher
entries.description: The recent-apps view: shrunken cards of open apps laid out side by side or stacked, ready to be swiped away. Distinct from [app_icon_grid](#app_icon_grid), which shows launchers rather than running screens.

entries.name: call_screen
entries.description: A voice call: caller name or number large in the middle, mute, speaker and hang-up buttons below, or the incoming ring with accept and decline. Use [video_call_screen](#video_call_screen) when a camera feed is showing.

entries.name: home_screen_widget
entries.description: A panel sitting among the icons showing live content: weather, a calendar strip, a clock, a music tile. Use this for the small embedded card; the full app it belongs to gets its own tag, such as weather or calendar screens.

entries.name: mobile_browser_screen
entries.description: A web page seen in a phone browser: a narrow address bar at the top or bottom and a single-column page below. Use [web_page_screenshot](#web_page_screenshot) for the desktop-width capture with full browser chrome.

entries.name: mobile_payment_screen
entries.description: A payment or banking app mid-transaction: an amount in large type, a recipient, and a confirm or slide-to-pay control. Use [receipt](#receipt) for the record that comes afterwards, whether paper or emailed.

entries.name: read_receipt
entries.description: The delivery and seen marks under or beside a sent message: double ticks, a "Read" label, a small avatar. Worth tagging when the receipts are the point of the [screenshot](#screenshot).

entries.name: share_sheet
entries.description: The panel that slides up from the bottom offering apps and actions to send something to, usually a row of contacts over a row of app icons. Distinct from [context_menu](#context_menu), which appears at the point of a long press.

entries.name: splash_screen
entries.description: The holding screen an app shows while it starts: a centred logo or mark on a flat background, sometimes a spinner. Use [boot_screen](#boot_screen) for the operating system starting up rather than a single app.

entries.name: story_view
entries.description: A full-bleed picture or clip filling the screen with progress segments across the top and a reply field at the bottom. Tag [vertical_video_player](#vertical_video_player) for the endless swipe-up video feed, which has no segment bar.

entries.name: typing_indicator
entries.description: The three animated dots or the "typing…" line showing the other person is composing a reply. A small detail, but it dates the capture to a live conversation rather than scrollback.

entries.name: vertical_video_player
entries.description: A short video filling a portrait screen with a caption low-left and a column of icons down the right edge. Use [music_player_screen](#music_player_screen) for audio playback and [story_view](#story_view) when segment bars run across the top.

entries.name: voice_message
entries.description: A message shown as a waveform or bar with a play button and a duration instead of text. Tag it when at least one such clip is visible in the thread; a call in progress is [call_screen](#call_screen).

entries.name: qr_code_scanner
entries.description: The camera pointed at a code with a framing bracket or highlight drawn over it, sometimes with the decoded link as a chip. Tag [camera_viewfinder](#camera_viewfinder) alone when the camera is just taking a picture.

entries.name: game_screenshot
entries.description: A capture of a running game, whether rendered 3D, 2D sprites or text. Use it for anything grabbed from play, including menus and cutscenes. For a photograph of a screen with a game on it, tag the photograph instead.

entries.name: video_frame_grab
entries.description: A still lifted out of moving footage, often with compression blocking, motion blur or interlacing. Use it for frames pulled from film, television or clips. If player controls or a progress bar show, add [streaming_player](#streaming_player).

entries.name: dashboard
entries.description: A single screen of tiles reporting the state of something: counters, small charts, status lights and a filter bar. Use it for analytics, monitoring and admin panels. A slide built to be presented is [presentation_slide](#presentation_slide).

entries.name: game_hud
entries.description: Gameplay with the status overlay visible: health bars, ammo, timers, crosshair, quest markers. Use it when the interface is part of what the picture shows. A shot taken with the overlay hidden is [photo_mode_capture](#photo_mode_capture) or a plain [game_screenshot](#game_screenshot).

entries.name: presentation_slide
entries.description: One slide from a deck: a heading with bullets, an image, or a chart, sized to a wide frame. Use it whether exported, screenshotted or photographed off a projector. The opening slide is [title_slide](#title_slide).

entries.name: streaming_player
entries.description: Video with the player interface showing: scrubber, elapsed time, volume, quality and fullscreen buttons. Use it for web and app players alike. A clean frame with no controls is [video_frame_grab](#video_frame_grab).

entries.name: subtitle_frame
entries.description: A video still with a caption line across the lower part of the picture, burned in or rendered by the player. Use it for dubs, translations and closed captions. Game speech panels are [dialogue_box](#dialogue_box).

entries.name: ui_mockup
entries.description: A designed screen that was never running: real colours, type and imagery laid out in a design tool. Use it for polished visual comps. A grey box-and-line sketch is [wireframe](#wireframe).

entries.name: video_call_screenshot
entries.description: A meeting window: a grid of participant tiles or one speaker with thumbnails, plus mute and leave controls. Use it for one-to-one calls too. A shared document or slide fills [screen_share_frame](#screen_share_frame) instead.

entries.name: wireframe
entries.description: A low-fidelity layout in greys and outlines: boxes for images, ruled lines for text, no real content. Often annotated. Once colour and real type arrive it is a [ui_mockup](#ui_mockup).

entries.name: dialogue_box
