entries.description: A speech panel over the scene with a speaker name, typed-out line and often reply choices. Common in role-playing games and visual novels. Burned-in film or video subtitles are [subtitle_frame](#subtitle_frame).

entries.name: letterboxed_frame
entries.description: A frame with black bars filling the space the picture does not use: top and bottom for wide film on a narrower screen, left and right for the reverse. Note the bars belong to the file, not to the display.

entries.name: loading_screen
entries.description: A waiting screen between scenes: a progress bar, spinning icon, tip text or splash art. Use it for game and application loads alike. Stalled video playback is [buffering_screen](#buffering_screen).

entries.name: lower_third
entries.description: The name-and-role strip laid over the bottom of a broadcast frame, often a coloured bar with two lines of text. Use it for on-screen graphics of that shape generally. A scrolling headline strip is [news_ticker](#news_ticker).

entries.name: media_library_grid
entries.description: The browse view of a video, music or game service: rows of cover art with titles, a featured banner across the top. Use it for local library apps as well. Playback itself is [streaming_player](#streaming_player).

entries.name: screen_share_frame
entries.description: Someone else's screen relayed inside a call or stream, usually with a border, a presenter strip and a small camera tile in a corner. The double framing is the giveaway. A plain capture of your own screen is not this.

entries.name: title_card
entries.description: A frame that exists to carry text: the title over a held shot, an episode name, a chapter marker or a location caption. Use it for intertitles as well. Rolling names at the end are [end_credits](#end_credits).

entries.name: title_screen
entries.description: The opening screen of a game: logo art with Start, Continue and Options. Use it for the main [menu](#menu) reached from that screen too. A menu opened mid-play is [pause_menu](#pause_menu).

entries.name: achievement_popup
entries.description: The small toast that slides in when a trophy, [badge](#badge) or level unlocks, with an icon and a short line of text. Tag it when the popup is what the capture was taken for.

entries.name: character_creation_screen
entries.description: A character standing in a blank studio surrounded by sliders, presets and colour swatches. Use it for appearance editors and class or origin pickers. An avatar shown only to change gear is [inventory_screen](#inventory_screen).

entries.name: end_credits
entries.description: The credit roll or crawl of names and roles, usually pale text on black. Use it for the static credit cards at the head of a film as well.

entries.name: game_over_screen
entries.description: The failure or end-of-run screen: a death message, retry prompt, or a run summary with score and time. Use it for victory and results screens too when they close out a session.

entries.name: inventory_screen
entries.description: A grid or list of carried items, equipment slots, stats or a skill tree. Use it for any full-screen management panel a game opens over play. A small persistent item bar belongs to [game_hud](#game_hud).

entries.name: leaderboard
entries.description: A ranked [table](#table) of players with scores, times or ratings. Use it for in-game high-score boards and standings pages alike. A tally shown during play, such as a match scoreline, is [game_hud](#game_hud).

entries.name: livestream_chat_overlay
entries.description: A live broadcast with the viewer chat column or floating messages, alerts and emotes over the picture. Common over gameplay. If only the game and its interface show, use [game_hud](#game_hud).

entries.name: minimap
entries.description: The small corner [map](#map) with player arrow, icons and a compass edge. Tag it when the minimap is the point of the picture, not merely present. A full-screen world map is a separate panel.

entries.name: news_ticker
entries.description: The band of scrolling headlines, scores or prices along the bottom edge of a broadcast. Often paired with a clock and a channel mark. A static caption naming a speaker is [lower_third](#lower_third).

entries.name: pause_menu
entries.description: Play halted with the options list over a dimmed or frozen scene: [resume](#resume), settings, quit. Distinguish from [title_screen](#title_screen), which is the [menu](#menu) before a session starts.

entries.name: photo_mode_capture
entries.description: A game image composed deliberately with the interface hidden, often with depth of field, a filter or a free camera. It looks like a photograph until you notice the render. If any status overlay shows, use [game_hud](#game_hud).

entries.name: picture_in_picture
entries.description: A small video panel inset into a larger picture: a floating player over a page, a camera tile over gameplay, or an inset speaker over footage. The inset has its own frame and often its own controls.

entries.name: prototype_flow
entries.description: Several screens laid side by side on a board with arrows or links showing the path between them. Use it for user-flow boards and clickable prototype canvases. One screen on its own is [ui_mockup](#ui_mockup) or [wireframe](#wireframe).

entries.name: title_slide
entries.description: The opening slide of a deck: a talk or product name, sometimes a speaker, date and logo, with little else on it. Section dividers inside a deck count too.

entries.name: video_editing_timeline
entries.description: An editing workspace: stacked video and audio tracks with clips and waveforms, a playhead, and a preview pane above. Use it for audio editors as well. The finished output played back is [streaming_player](#streaming_player).

entries.name: buffering_screen
entries.description: Playback stalled: a spinner or percentage over a frozen or blacked-out frame, sometimes with an error line. Use it for playback failures too. A game or app starting up is [loading_screen](#loading_screen).

entries.name: slide_sorter_view
entries.description: A deck seen as a grid or filmstrip of small slides in the editing tool, with the running order visible. Use it when the deck as a whole is the subject rather than any one slide.

entries.name: whiteboard
entries.description: A wipeable white panel written on with dry-erase markers, usually in an office or classroom. Use [blackboard](#blackboard) when the surface is dark and the writing is chalk, and [interactive_whiteboard](#interactive_whiteboard) when the board is a display driven by a computer.

entries.name: blackboard
entries.description: A dark slate or painted board written on in chalk, with the smeared grey haze an eraser leaves behind. Covers green school boards as well as black ones; use [whiteboard](#whiteboard) for the marker-and-wipe kind.

entries.name: whiteboard_diagram
entries.description: Boxes, arrows, sketched architecture or a scribbled explanation drawn on a board rather than typed. Use it for the drawn content; [board_equations](#board_equations) covers a board filled with mathematics instead.

entries.name: bullet_slide
entries.description: A slide whose body is a list of short lines under a heading, the plainest and most common deck page. Use [lecture_slide](#lecture_slide) when it is dense academic material and [title_slide](#title_slide) for an opening page.

entries.name: chalk_writing
entries.description: Text or drawing made in chalk, dusty-edged and slightly translucent, rather than the flat opaque line of a marker. Use it for the marks themselves; [blackboard](#blackboard) is for the surface, and it is worth tagging both.

entries.name: flipchart
entries.description: A large paper pad on a stand, written on a sheet at a time and flipped over or torn off. The sheets are often taped to a wall afterwards. Use [whiteboard](#whiteboard) for a wipeable surface and [poster_board](#poster_board) for a rigid display panel.

entries.name: kanban_board
entries.description: Work items arranged in labelled vertical columns such as to do, doing and done, drawn on a board or shown on a screen. Tag [sticky_note_wall](#sticky_note_wall) as well when the cards are physical notes without any column structure.

entries.name: lectern
entries.description: The slanted reading stand a speaker talks from, usually with a microphone and a small light. Use [easel](#easel) for a stand holding a board or pad, and [conference_stage](#conference_stage) for the wider view of the platform.

entries.name: lecture_slide
entries.description: A teaching slide, typically dense with text, figures, citations or equations and carrying a course or unit number. Use [bullet_slide](#bullet_slide) for an ordinary sparse business page.

entries.name: pinboard
entries.description: A soft cork or fabric panel holding paper down with pins or tacks, layered and overlapping. Use [sticky_note_wall](#sticky_note_wall) when the notes are self-adhesive squares stuck straight to a surface, and [letter_board](#letter_board) for slotted characters.

entries.name: projected_image
entries.description: Light cast from a projector onto a surface, washed out at the edges and often crossed by a presenter's shadow. Tag [projector_screen](#projector_screen) as well when a proper screen is in the frame; use [photo_of_a_screen](#photo_of_a_screen) for a display photographed directly.

entries.name: projector_screen
entries.description: The white or grey sheet a projector throws onto, pulled down or on a tripod frame, with its border and hanging weight visible. Use [projected_image](#projected_image) when the picture is cast straight onto a wall with no screen.

entries.name: speaker_at_lectern
entries.description: A person mid-talk behind a stand, lit from the front with a slide or screen behind them. Use [lectern](#lectern) alone when the stand is empty, and [conference_stage](#conference_stage) when the framing is the whole platform rather than the speaker.

entries.name: sticky_note_wall
entries.description: A field of small self-adhesive notes stuck to a wall, window or board, usually in colour blocks from a workshop. Use [kanban_board](#kanban_board) when the notes sit in labelled columns, and [pinboard](#pinboard) when paper is held by pins instead.

entries.name: agenda_slide
entries.description: A numbered [outline](#outline) of what the talk will cover, sometimes repeated with the current section highlighted. Distinguished from [bullet_slide](#bullet_slide), which carries actual content rather than a roadmap.

entries.name: board_equations
entries.description: A board covered in handwritten mathematics, derivations or formulae, often running across several panels. Use [whiteboard_diagram](#whiteboard_diagram) when the content is boxes and arrows rather than notation.

entries.name: conference_stage
entries.description: A wide view of a talk venue: a lit platform, a large screen behind it and the backs of an audience in the foreground. Use [speaker_at_lectern](#speaker_at_lectern) for a tighter shot of the person and [poster_session](#poster_session) for the informal panel format.

entries.name: easel
entries.description: A folding tripod or A-frame stand holding a pad, board or panel upright for an audience. Tag it when the stand itself is visible in the frame; what sits on it usually gets its own tag, such as [flipchart](#flipchart) or [poster_board](#poster_board).

entries.name: handout
entries.description: Printed pages given to an audience, often slides shrunk several to a sheet with ruled lines for notes. Use [presentation_slide](#presentation_slide) for the full-size page and [poster_board](#poster_board) for a standing display.

entries.name: interactive_whiteboard
entries.description: A large touch display used as a board, showing a bright rendered surface with an on-screen toolbar and crisp digital ink. Use [whiteboard](#whiteboard) for a physical marker surface and [projector_screen](#projector_screen) when a projector throws the image onto a passive sheet.

entries.name: letter_board
entries.description: A grooved felt or plastic panel with individual characters slotted in by hand, giving uneven spacing and a soft drop shadow. Use [pinboard](#pinboard) for pinned paper and [blackboard](#blackboard) for chalk lettering.

entries.name: poster_board
entries.description: A rigid standing display panel carrying a printed [poster](#poster) or pinned sheets, often a folding trifold. Use [poster_session](#poster_session) for the room full of them, and [pinboard](#pinboard) for a soft wall-mounted cork panel.

entries.name: poster_session
entries.description: A hall of research posters on freestanding panels with people standing beside them talking. Use [poster_board](#poster_board) for the display panel on its own and [conference_stage](#conference_stage) for a talk given from a platform.

entries.name: presenter_view
entries.description: The speaker's own screen during a talk: the current slide beside the next one, a timer and typed speaker notes. Use [presentation_slide](#presentation_slide) for the plain audience-facing page.

entries.name: slide_sorter
entries.description: A whole deck shown as a grid of small slide thumbnails for reordering. Tag it rather than [presentation_slide](#presentation_slide) when many pages are visible at once and none is readable on its own.

entries.name: laser_pointer
entries.description: A hard red or green dot on a screen or board, usually with a bright bloom around it, from a presenter's pointer. Rare but distinctive; tag it alongside whatever surface the dot lands on.

entries.name: overhead_projector
entries.description: The older lamp-and-mirror machine that throws a hand-marked transparency sheet onto a wall. Recognisable by the arm above the glass platen; use [projector_screen](#projector_screen) and [projected_image](#projected_image) for modern digital projection.

entries.name: string_board
entries.description: Pinned photographs and clippings joined by lengths of taut yarn to show connections between them. A narrow, dramatic use of a [pinboard](#pinboard); tag plain pinned notices as pinboard alone.

entries.name: photographed_document
entries.description: A page shot with a camera or phone rather than run through a scanner. Lighting is uneven, the surround is visible, and the page usually sits at an angle. Use [scanned_document](#scanned_document) for a flat, evenly lit capture.

entries.name: scanned_document
entries.description: A page digitised on a scanner rather than photographed: even lighting, no perspective, edges parallel to the frame. Use [photographed_document](#photographed_document) when a camera was held over the page instead.

entries.name: phone_scan
entries.description: A handheld phone capture of a page, often cropped and straightened by a scanning app so it imitates a real scan. Look for a slightly warped baseline and blown edges; a true [flatbed_scan](#flatbed_scan) has neither.

entries.name: shadow_across_page
entries.description: A shadow falls over part of the sheet, darkening one region while the rest stays bright. Use [photographer_shadow](#photographer_shadow) when the shape of the person or phone is recognisable, [uneven_lighting](#uneven_lighting) for a soft gradient with no edge.

entries.name: skewed_page
entries.description: The page is rotated in the frame: text lines run at an angle instead of horizontally, but the sheet is still rectangular. Rotation only — use [keystoned_page](#keystoned_page) when the edges converge.

entries.name: top_down_capture
entries.description: Shot straight down on the page so the sheet stays rectangular and the text baselines run level. The clean counterpart to [angled_capture](#angled_capture); it does not mean the page is flat.

entries.name: angled_capture
entries.description: The camera sits off to one side or low over the page, so the sheet reads as a trapezoid and one edge is nearer than the other. When the convergence is strong enough to distort the text, add [keystoned_page](#keystoned_page).

entries.name: blurry_text
entries.description: The writing is soft enough to be hard or impossible to read, from missed focus or too little light. Use [motion_blur](#motion_blur) when the smear runs in one direction; use [pixelated_text](#pixelated_text) when the letters are blocky rather than soft.

entries.name: cropped_to_page
entries.description: Trimmed exactly to the sheet, with nothing of the desk, scanner bed or holding hand left in frame. Typical of scanning apps. If the crop bites into the text, use [cut_off_text](#cut_off_text) instead.

entries.name: curled_page
entries.description: A loose sheet that will not lie flat — a [receipt](#receipt) rolling up, a photograph cupping, a corner lifting off the desk. Use [page_curvature](#page_curvature) for the bend of a bound page near its spine.

entries.name: cut_off_text
entries.description: Words are sliced by the edge of the frame or the crop, so lines cannot be read to their end. A capture fault; [partial_page](#partial_page) is the neutral tag for showing only a section on purpose.

entries.name: document_on_desk
entries.description: The sheet is lying on a [table](#table), floor or other surface that is visible around it, rather than filling the frame. Tag the setting, not the angle — pair it with [top_down_capture](#top_down_capture) or [angled_capture](#angled_capture).

entries.name: flatbed_scan
entries.description: Scanned face-down on a glass bed, so the page is pressed flat and the background behind it is a flat white or black field. Book scans done this way usually show [gutter_shadow](#gutter_shadow) along the spine.

entries.name: glare_on_page
entries.description: A bright reflection of a lamp, window or ceiling light sits on the paper and washes out whatever is under it. Especially bad on glossy or laminated stock. Use [flash_glare](#flash_glare) for the hard hotspot of an on-camera flash.

entries.name: hand_holding_page
entries.description: A hand appears in the picture holding, flattening or turning the document. Use [finger_over_text](#finger_over_text) when the hand actually covers words rather than just gripping an edge.

entries.name: multi_page_spread
entries.description: Two facing pages of an open book, magazine or [passport](#passport) captured in one frame, with the gutter running between them. One page alone, however wide, is not a spread.

entries.name: partial_page
entries.description: Only part of the sheet is in frame, whether deliberately zoomed on one section or simply framed short. The document continues past the picture edge in at least one direction.

entries.name: photocopy
entries.description: A copier reproduction rather than a digital capture: crushed greys, a hard black edge where the lid did not close, dropped-out faint marks. Tag the copy itself, not a scan of an original.

entries.name: uneven_lighting
entries.description: The page is lit brighter on one side than the other, or falls off toward the corners, with no shadow edge you can point at. Use [shadow_across_page](#shadow_across_page) when something is clearly casting a shadow.

entries.name: yellowed_paper
entries.description: The stock has aged to a warm cream or brown, often darkest at the edges. A property of the paper, so it survives any capture method; a warm cast from tungsten light is not this.

entries.name: bleed_through
entries.description: Print or writing from the reverse of the sheet shows through as faint mirrored marks between the lines. Typical of thin paper on a backlit or white-backed scan; a black backing sheet suppresses it.

entries.name: crumpled_page
entries.description: The paper has been balled up or crushed, leaving a dense web of random wrinkles and a surface that will not flatten. Use [creased_page](#creased_page) for a few deliberate folds.

entries.name: fax
entries.description: A page transmitted and printed by fax: coarse bitonal rendering, stretched or skewed lines, a header strip across the top. Distinct from [photocopy](#photocopy), which keeps grey tones.

entries.name: finger_over_text
entries.description: A finger or thumb lies across the printed area and hides part of what the page says. A capture fault worth flagging separately from [hand_holding_page](#hand_holding_page), where the grip stays clear of the text.

entries.name: flash_glare
entries.description: A hard, roughly circular hotspot from the camera's own flash, usually near the centre of the sheet, with the corners falling off dark. A particular kind of [glare_on_page](#glare_on_page).

entries.name: gutter_shadow
entries.description: A dark band down the centre of an open book where the pages fall away into the spine and the light cannot reach. Common on a [flatbed_scan](#flatbed_scan) of a bound volume; it usually comes with [page_curvature](#page_curvature).

entries.name: keystoned_page
entries.description: Perspective makes the page a trapezoid: the far edge is shorter than the near one and lines of text taper. Caused by [angled_capture](#angled_capture); [skewed_page](#skewed_page) is plain rotation without any taper.

entries.name: low_contrast_scan
entries.description: Ink and paper sit close together in tone, giving a flat grey page that is tiring to read and awkward to threshold. Often a scanner setting rather than the state of the paper; [faded_print](#faded_print) is the paper's own fault.

entries.name: moire_pattern
entries.description: Interference ripples or a coloured crosshatch where the capture grid beats against a printed halftone or a display's pixels. An artefact of the capture, never something on the page itself.

entries.name: motion_blur
entries.description: Camera or page moved during the exposure, so letters trail in a single direction and edges double. Directional; [blurry_text](#blurry_text) is the general soft, non-directional case.

entries.name: overexposed_page
entries.description: The paper is blown to pure white and light strokes, rules or pencil marks have disappeared into it. A whole-page exposure problem, unlike [glare_on_page](#glare_on_page), which burns out one patch.

entries.name: overhead_scan
entries.description: Captured by a camera or scan head mounted above an open book or loose sheet, so the page is never pressed flat. Expect [page_curvature](#page_curvature) near the spine; a [flatbed_scan](#flatbed_scan) flattens it instead.

entries.name: page_corner_visible
entries.description: One or more corners of the sheet sit inside the frame against the surface behind it, showing where the page ends. Useful to distinguish a real object shot from a borderless scan.

entries.name: page_curvature
entries.description: The sheet bows away from the camera near the binding, so the text bends and compresses toward the gutter. A property of bound pages; [curled_page](#curled_page) is for a loose sheet rolling at its edges.

entries.name: photographer_shadow
entries.description: The silhouette of the person or the phone doing the capturing lands on the page. A specific, recognisable case of [shadow_across_page](#shadow_across_page) and a good sign the picture is a handheld capture.

entries.name: pixelated_text
entries.description: Captured or saved at too low a resolution: letterforms break into visible blocks and small type turns to mush. Distinct from [blurry_text](#blurry_text), where the strokes are soft rather than square.

entries.name: scan_artifacts
entries.description: Faults introduced by the scanner: dust specks, hairline scratches, a streak or band running the length of the sheet, banding from a dirty glass. Damage on the paper itself belongs to [stained_page](#stained_page) or [torn_page](#torn_page).

entries.name: microfilm_scan
entries.description: Digitised from film rather than from paper: high-contrast, often white-on-black, with film grain and frame edges. Use it only when the film intermediate is visible, not for any old newspaper page.

entries.name: printed_text
entries.description: Text set in type and printed or laser-printed, with even letterforms and a regular baseline. The default for most documents. Use [handwritten_text](#handwritten_text) when a person wrote it by hand, and [typewritten](#typewritten) for the uneven inked strike of a typewriter.

entries.name: dense_text
entries.description: A page packed edge to edge with running text, little white space and few breaks. Useful for finding walls of prose to skip or to crop. Use [columns_of_text](#columns_of_text) when the block is clearly divided into vertical columns.

entries.name: handwritten_signature
entries.description: A signed name, usually on a rule or in a [signature](#signature) block, written more quickly and loosely than the rest of the writing. Tag the signature itself; use [stamped](#stamped) for a facsimile applied with a stamp.

entries.name: handwritten_text
entries.description: Writing made by hand with pen, pencil or brush, letterforms varying from one to the next. Covers notes, filled-in forms and inscriptions. Use [printed_text](#printed_text) for anything set in type, and [calligraphy](#calligraphy) when the hand is deliberately decorative.

entries.name: bulleted_list
entries.description: Short lines marked with dots, dashes or numbers and indented as a list rather than run together as prose. Tag the list setting itself. Use [dense_text](#dense_text) for continuous paragraphs and [section_heading](#section_heading) for the label above a block.

entries.name: columns_of_text
entries.description: The text is set in two or more vertical columns separated by gutters, as in newspapers, journals and reference works. Tag the layout regardless of what the page is. Use [dense_text](#dense_text) for an undivided slab of prose.

entries.name: crossed_out_text
entries.description: Words struck through with a line, scribble or row of x's, marking them as deleted while still visible. Common on drafts and corrected forms. Use [redacted_text](#redacted_text) when the point is to make the words unreadable.

entries.name: fine_print
entries.description: Very small type, usually terms, disclaimers or footnote-sized matter, often barely legible at the picture's resolution. Tag the size of the setting, not the subject. Use [illegible_text](#illegible_text) when nothing can be read at all.

entries.name: highlighted_text
entries.description: Words marked with a translucent colour band from a highlighter pen or a digital tool, still readable through it. Tag any colour, not just yellow. Use [redacted_text](#redacted_text) when the marking hides the words instead of emphasising them.

entries.name: large_print
entries.description: Text set unusually big for its medium, so few words fill the frame — large-print editions, notices, signage-style sheets. Judge it against what the document would normally use. The opposite case is [fine_print](#fine_print).

entries.name: margin_notes
entries.description: Comments, corrections or arrows written into the margins or between the lines of an existing document. Tag the annotation layer, not the underlying page. Use [proofreading_marks](#proofreading_marks) when the marks are the standard correction symbols.

entries.name: page_numbers
entries.description: Folios printed in a corner or centred at the head or foot of the page. Useful for telling a numbered page apart from a loose sheet. Use [running_head](#running_head) for the repeated title line that often sits beside them.

entries.name: redacted_text
entries.description: Passages blacked out with solid bars or blocks so the words underneath cannot be read, leaving the surrounding text intact. Tag the deliberate covering. Use [highlighted_text](#highlighted_text) for translucent colour that leaves words readable.

entries.name: section_heading
entries.description: A line set larger, bolder or in a contrasting face to open a section, standing apart from the body text below it. Tag the treatment on the page, not the document's title page. Compare [running_head](#running_head) for the small repeated line at the top of every page.

entries.name: stamped
entries.description: An inked stamp impression sitting on top of the text — dates, PAID, APPROVED, a receiving mark — often crooked and in a different colour. Tag the impression wherever it lands. Use [embossed_seal](#embossed_seal) for a raised, uninked mark.

entries.name: underlined_text
entries.description: A line drawn or set beneath words for emphasis, by hand or in the typesetting. Includes double and wavy rules. Use [crossed_out_text](#crossed_out_text) for a line through the letters and [highlighted_text](#highlighted_text) for a colour band over them.

entries.name: block_capitals
entries.description: Text written or set entirely in separated upright capital letters, common on forms, labels and signs. Use it for the letterform itself, not for emphasis inside a body of running text. Compare [cursive](#cursive) for joined-up hand.

entries.name: calligraphy
entries.description: Lettering drawn as a deliberate art, with controlled stroke weight and flourishes — invitations, certificates, inscriptions. Use [handwritten_text](#handwritten_text) for ordinary writing and [blackletter](#blackletter) when the same look is printed type rather than a drawn hand.

entries.name: circled_text
entries.description: A word, figure or block ringed by hand to single it out, sometimes with an arrow leading away from it. Tag the ring itself. Use [margin_notes](#margin_notes) when the marking includes written comments in the margin.

entries.name: cursive
entries.description: Joined-up handwriting where letters flow into one another without lifting the pen. Often harder to read than print hand. Use [block_capitals](#block_capitals) for separated upright letters and [calligraphy](#calligraphy) when the script is a decorative performance rather than everyday writing.

entries.name: embossed_seal
entries.description: A mark pressed into the paper so it stands in relief, readable by its shadow rather than by ink — notarial and institutional seals. Use [stamped](#stamped) for an inked impression and [watermarked_document](#watermarked_document) for a mark held inside the sheet.

entries.name: footnotes
entries.description: Small notes keyed by superscript marks and set at the foot of the page, usually below a rule. Tag the presence of the apparatus. Use [fine_print](#fine_print) when the whole page is set small rather than just this band.

entries.name: justified_text
entries.description: Lines flush at both margins, with word spacing stretched to fit, sometimes leaving visible rivers of white. Tag it when the even right edge is a plain feature of the setting; ragged-right text needs no tag.

entries.name: monospaced_text
entries.description: Type where every character occupies the same width, so columns of letters line up down the page. Common in code listings, tables and technical printouts. Use [typewritten](#typewritten) if the page actually came out of a typewriter.

entries.name: reversed_out_text
entries.description: Light type on a dark ground — white words in a black bar, a knocked-out heading, a solid panel of inverted text. Tag the tonal reversal of the setting, not a photographic negative of the whole page.

entries.name: running_head
entries.description: A small repeated line at the top or bottom of every page carrying the title, chapter or section, often with a rule under it. Tag it separately from [page_numbers](#page_numbers), which may sit on the same line.

entries.name: typewritten
entries.description: Text struck by a typewriter: fixed-width letters, uneven ink density, sometimes visible impressions in the paper. Distinct from [monospaced_text](#monospaced_text), which is a computer typeface imitating the same rhythm on clean output.

entries.name: vertical_writing
entries.description: Lines running from top to bottom of the page, columns read right to left, as in traditional East Asian setting — or roman type turned on its side in a [table](#table) or spine. Tag the direction of the lines.

entries.name: watermarked_document
entries.description: A pale word or device laid across the page — DRAFT, COPY, CONFIDENTIAL, a house mark — either printed under the text or held in the paper itself. Use [stamped](#stamped) for a solid inked impression added afterwards.

entries.name: blackletter
entries.description: Dense angular gothic type with heavy strokes and pointed terminals, seen on old books, certificates and mastheads. Tag the typeface itself. Use [calligraphy](#calligraphy) only when the letters were drawn by hand rather than printed.

entries.name: drop_cap
entries.description: An opening [letter](#letter) set several lines deep, sunk into the first paragraph, sometimes decorated or coloured. Common in books and older printing. Use [section_heading](#section_heading) for an ordinary bold line opening a section.

entries.name: lorem_ipsum
entries.description: Placeholder or dummy copy standing in for real words in a layout, the same pseudo-Latin or repeated phrases filling every block. Tag it wherever the text is filler rather than content, printed or on screen.

entries.name: mirrored_text
entries.description: Text reversed left to right, as when a page is shot through the back, seen in a mirror, or scanned from a transfer. Reads correctly only when flipped. Use [vertical_writing](#vertical_writing) for text running down the page rather than reversed.

entries.name: proofreading_marks
entries.description: The standard correction symbols of typesetting — deletion loops, carets, transposition marks, stet — worked into the text and margins. A narrower case of [margin_notes](#margin_notes); use that tag for ordinary written comments.

entries.name: shorthand
entries.description: Stenographic writing in abbreviated symbols and strokes rather than letters, seen in notebooks and dictation pads. Unreadable without the system, but regular and rhythmic, unlike the broken scrawl of [illegible_text](#illegible_text).

entries.name: legible_text
entries.description: Every word in the picture can be read without guessing. Use it to mark a shot that is good enough to transcribe or search; if only part of the writing resolves, use [partially_legible](#partially_legible) instead.

entries.name: blurred_text
entries.description: Letters are soft and smeared, from missed focus or camera shake. Distinct from [low_resolution_text](#low_resolution_text), where the letters are sharp-edged but built from too few pixels.

entries.name: creased_page
entries.description: One or more sharp fold lines cross the sheet, often with the ink cracked along them. A page carrying many random wrinkles rather than deliberate folds is [crumpled_page](#crumpled_page).

entries.name: cropped_text
entries.description: Words run off the edge of the frame, so lines are cut short or a margin is missing. About framing, not damage; a physically absent piece of paper is [torn_page](#torn_page).

entries.name: faded_print
entries.description: Ink or toner has thinned with age, light or a failing printer, leaving pale and patchy characters. The loss is in the marks themselves, not in the lighting, which is [low_contrast_text](#low_contrast_text).

entries.name: glare
entries.description: A specular reflection lies across the surface and hides the text under it, on glossy paper, laminate or a screen. Reserve [overexposed_page](#overexposed_page) for a whole sheet lost to light rather than one bright streak.

entries.name: illegible_text
entries.description: Writing is visible as writing but cannot be read at all. Say why with a second tag where you can, such as [blurred_text](#blurred_text) or [faded_print](#faded_print); if some of it still reads, use [partially_legible](#partially_legible).

entries.name: low_contrast_text
entries.description: The ink and the paper sit close together in tone, so the writing is present but weak. Use [faded_print](#faded_print) when the ink itself has worn away, and this when the exposure or the original printing was simply flat.

entries.name: low_resolution_text
entries.description: The lettering breaks into visible pixels or blocky steps because the capture is too small for the type size. Edges stay hard, unlike [blurred_text](#blurred_text); a photographed screen may show [moire_pattern](#moire_pattern) as well.

entries.name: obscured_text
entries.description: Something in front of the page covers the writing: a finger, a pen, a sticky note, another sheet. The text is intact underneath, unlike [redacted_text](#redacted_text), where it was deliberately blacked out.

entries.name: partially_legible
entries.description: Some of the text reads and some does not, whether from damage, framing or focus. The middle ground between [legible_text](#legible_text) and [illegible_text](#illegible_text), and the right tag for most imperfect page shots.

entries.name: skewed_text
entries.description: The lines run at an angle to the frame because the page or the scanner was rotated. Flat rotation only; convergence from shooting a page at an angle is [keystoned_page](#keystoned_page).

entries.name: stained_page
entries.description: Coffee, grease, dirt or an unknown liquid has left coloured marks on the sheet. For overall age discolouration use [yellowed_paper](#yellowed_paper), and for rippled sheets with tide lines use [water_damaged](#water_damaged).

entries.name: torn_page
entries.description: Paper is physically ripped, with a missing piece or a tear crossing the text. Use it for absent material; words merely outside the frame are [cropped_text](#cropped_text).

entries.name: binding_curve
entries.description: Text bends and darkens as it runs into the spine of a bound book, the inner words compressed or lost. Typical of a phone shot of an open volume; a flat single sheet cannot show it.

entries.name: cracked_screen
entries.description: The display is broken: spidering cracks, black blotches or coloured bands crossing what is on screen. Use it when the damage is what makes the text hard to read.

entries.name: ink_bleed
entries.description: Ink has spread into the paper fibres, thickening strokes and blurring counters until small type closes up. Symmetrical spread around each mark; a directional streak is [smudged_ink](#smudged_ink).

entries.name: show_through
entries.description: Printing from the back of the sheet is visible through thin paper and interferes with the side you are reading. Mirror-reversed text under the real text is the giveaway.

entries.name: smudged_ink
entries.description: Wet ink has been dragged across the surface by a hand or a sleeve, trailing the letters sideways. The smear direction is visible, unlike [ink_bleed](#ink_bleed), which spreads outward into the fibres.

entries.name: water_damaged
entries.description: The sheet has been wet: rippled or cockled paper, tide lines at the edge of the wetted area, ink run or dissolved. Stronger and more specific than a plain [stained_page](#stained_page).

entries.name: burned_edges
entries.description: The sheet is scorched, with charred brown or black borders and text lost at the burn line. Rare and unmistakable; do not use it for paper merely darkened by age, which is [yellowed_paper](#yellowed_paper).

entries.name: foxed_paper
entries.description: Small rust-brown speckles are scattered across old paper, the mould and metal spotting called foxing. Discrete dots, unlike the flat overall tone of [yellowed_paper](#yellowed_paper).

entries.name: toner_streaks
entries.description: Bands, stripes or repeating smears left by a failing printer or copier drum run down the page. A machine fault in the print itself, not a mark added afterwards like [smudged_ink](#smudged_ink).
